blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights how Amazon used a multi-armed bandit approach with Thompson sampling to optimize web page layouts in realtime, achieving a 21% increase in conversions within a week. The paper addresses the scalability limitations of traditional A/B testing when dealing with multivariate optimization problems, where the number of combinations grows exponentially. The authors propose a stochastic contextual multi-armed bandit model that balances exploration and exploitation, using a linear reward function and probit regression for binary outcomes. While the model theoretically accounts for contextual inputs and widget interactions, the production results showed that these features did not significantly improve performance over simpler baselines. The approach, dubbed MVT2, was deployed in a live setting and demonstrated substantial business value despite the lack of higher-order interactions in the tested scenario.
paper_title: An efficient bandit algorithm for realtime multivariate optimization
paper_abstract: Optimization. In Proceedings of KDD ’17, Halifax, NS, Canada, August 13-17, 2017, 9 pages. https://doi.org/10.1145/3097983.3098184 Optimization is commonly employed to determine the content of web pages, such as to maximize conversions on landing pages or click-through rates on search engine result pages. Often the layout of these pages can be decoupled into several separate decisions. For example, the composition of a landing page may involve deciding which image to show, which wording to use, what color background to display, etc. Such optimization is a combinatorial problem over an exponentially large decision space. Randomized experiments do not scale well to this setting, and therefore, in practice, one is typically limited to optimizing a single aspect of a web page at a time. This represents a missed opportunity in both the speed of experimentation and the exploitation of possible interactions between layout decisions. Here we focus on multivariate optimization of interactive web pages. We formulate an approach where the possible interactions between different components of the page are modeled explicitly. We apply bandit methodology to explore the layout space efficiently and use hill-climbing to select optimal content in realtime. Our algorithm also extends to contextualization and personalization of layout selection. Simulation results show the suitability of our approach to large decision spaces with strong interactions between content. We further apply our algorithm to optimize a message that promotes adoption of an Amazon service. After only a single week of online optimization, we saw a 21% conversion increase compared to the median layout. Our technique is currently being deployed to optimize content across several locations at Amazon.com.
